public_rationale: The claim is that current image generators, run many times on the same request, are sometimes right and sometimes wrong, and you cannot know in advance which you will get. A January 2025 study improves image models by trying many random starting points and keeping the better ones, which only works because quality varies from run to run. A 2025 evaluation of ChatGPT's GPT-4o image generator found it strong overall but still prone to errors in object-human interactions, the kind of scene in the post. A CVPR 2024 paper says plainly that not all random starts give images faithful to the prompt. Together these support the claim. One caveat: automated checkers can screen for better outputs, but a single run's result is still not known in advance.
limitations: The evidence is about the class of systems, not repeated runs of the exact prompt in ChatGPT-5 or Grok.
Automated checkers can partly filter outputs after generation, which softens 'you never know' for engineered pipelines.

our_interpretation: 'These systems' means the current generative image and video models discussed in the post, such as ChatGPT image generation and Grok.
Plain reading: the same request, run repeatedly, gives outputs that vary in correctness. Some are faithful and some are flawed, and a user cannot tell in advance which a given run will give.
The claim describes an ongoing state with no named period. I use 2025 up to the post date as the latest period public evidence could cover.
criteria.support_condition: Research from the period showing that a single prompt gives better or worse samples depending on random noise, or that leading 2025 systems are often but not always correct.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence that current systems give consistently correct (or consistently wrong) outputs for the same prompt, or that users can reliably predict the result of a run.
